analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug companies from paying generic and biosimilar rivals to delay launching cheaper copies.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have banned brand-name drug makers from paying generic competitors to stay off the market, never received a committee hearing or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic company challenges a drug patent and looks likely to win, brand-name drug makers sometimes settle the case by paying the generic company to stay out of the market for years — a practice called "pay for delay." This bill would make those deals unlawful. The FTC could sue violators for civil penalties of up to three times the deal's value, drug companies would have to file complete copies of every settlement with regulators, and a generic maker that took delay money would lose its valuable 180-day head start. The bill was referred to two House committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who pays for prescriptions — directly, through insurance premiums, or through taxes that fund Medicare and Medicaid. Banning pay-for-delay settlements means cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars reach the market on the timetable the patent law already allows, typically cutting prices substantially once competition arrives. Employers and insurers who pay for prescriptions also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for the maker of a brand-name drug to give anything of value to a generic or biosimilar applicant in exchange for delaying or giving up its plans to sell a competing product.

Violators face civil penalties of up to three times the value of the deal, and a generic maker that joins a prohibited deal forfeits its 180-day exclusivity period — the head start that makes being first-to-file valuable.

Drug companies must file complete copies of every settlement agreement with the FTC and the Justice Department, and a senior executive must certify under oath that nothing — including side deals or oral promises — was left out, making it harder to hide delay arrangements.
The FTC gets exclusive authority to sue violators as an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act, with civil penalties and injunctions available.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the ability to pay competitors to stay off the market and extend their years of high-priced exclusivity. A small number of generic manufacturers would lose the settlement payments they sometimes receive for agreeing to delay, and first-filing generic companies could forfeit their 180-day exclusivity if they join a prohibited deal.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers; some generic firms

drawbacks.text: The bill's exclusions are narrow: settlements are allowed only if the brand-name company grants an early license to market the drug, pays litigation costs capped at $7.5 million, or agrees not to sue. Settlements that involve payments for other business arrangements, like manufacturing or distribution help, would need clear and convincing proof that the value was only for those services — a standard that could chill legitimate cooperation.

Only the FTC could sue to enforce the ban, so if the agency chose not to act on a deal, private parties and state enforcers would have no path under this law (though existing antitrust claims are preserved).
A 6-year deadline on FTC enforcement, running from when the agreement is filed, could let deals that are structured to hide delay payments escape challenge if they are not detected in time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — lower drug prices through earlier generic and biosimilar competition — is broad and goes to consumers and insurers generally. The costs are narrow: brand-name companies would lose a settlement tool, and a few generic makers would lose deal payments. The main honest objection is that the exemptions may be too tight for legitimate settlements that pay generic makers to do something real, like co-develop or distribute the product, and the FTC's exclusive enforcement power means the law's strength depends on how aggressively the agency acts. On balance, the design directly targets a practice that keeps prices high, and the losers are the parties collecting the delay payments.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, then to a subcommittee, and neither committee ever held a hearing or vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 7, 2023 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees.
On November 10, 2023, the parts under Energy and Commerce's jurisdiction were referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce — the last recorded action.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill drew 3 cosponsors, all Democrats, which gave its committees little evidence of broader support to act on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers keep their ability to pay generic competitors to stay off the market, preserving higher prices and longer exclusivity; no patient benefit was delivered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers, whose higher prices continue

for.name: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 7, 2023, which would ban paying generic and biosimilar makers to delay market entry.

for.name: Reps. Sean Casten and Gerald Connolly
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and, over the remaining life of the Congress, never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took action on it.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry that benefits from pay-for-delay settlements
against.what_they_did: Brand-name drug manufacturers have long lobbied Congress against restrictions on patent-settlement agreements that delay generic entry; no such activity appears in this bill's congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic support — a sponsor and 3 Democratic cosponsors — and no Republican cosponsor ever joined, though no one is recorded as opposing it on the merits.

industries.note: These companies currently use patent settlements to pay would-be competitors to delay entry, extending their exclusive pricing years past the patent. The bill outlaws exactly that, with penalties up to three times the deal value.

First-filing generic companies would lose a lucrative option — being paid to wait — but would keep their 180-day exclusivity only by staying out of such deals, and would face a market where they can launch on schedule without pressure. Over time, more timely launches mean more products sold.

industries.industry: Consumers and payers (employers, insurers, government programs)
industries.note: Earlier generic and biosimilar entry typically cuts prices sharply once competition arrives. Patients paying out of pocket, employers, insurers, and Medicare all benefit when delay deals are blocked.
